territorial_scope.description: The bill applies to covered entities defined partly by the personal information of District residents, within the District's jurisdiction.

evidence.quote: Possesses or controls personal information on more than 25,000 District residents;

agora_harms: Violation of civil or human rights, including privacy

summary.short: The Stop Discrimination by Algorithms Act of 2023, a pending District of Columbia bill, would bar covered entities from making algorithmic eligibility or information-availability determinations based on protected traits in discriminatory ways. It would also require notices, adverse-action disclosures, annual audits, reports to the Attorney General, and civil enforcement. It would take effect after approval, congressional review and publication.
summary.long: The bill, introduced in the Council of the District of Columbia, prohibits covered entities from making algorithmic eligibility or algorithmic information availability determinations on the basis of protected traits in a manner that segregates, discriminates against, or makes important life opportunities unavailable (Sec. 4(a)). Practices with that effect are deemed unlawful discriminatory practices. Covered entities include those with personal information on more than 25,000 District residents, more than $15 million in average annualized gross receipts, data brokers meeting a revenue test, and service providers. Important life opportunities cover credit, education, employment, housing, public accommodations and insurance. Sec. 4(b) preserves Human Rights Act exemptions and affirmative action plans. Sec. 5 requires written agreements with service providers. Sec. 6 requires a public notice on personal information use, posting and pre-use delivery, and a disclosure to individuals after adverse actions based on eligibility determinations. Sec. 7 requires annual audits, an audit trail kept at least five years, annual impact assessments, and an annual report to the Attorney General. Sec. 8 authorizes Attorney General civil actions and investigations with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, and private civil actions with damages of $100 to $10,000 per violation or actual damages, plus punitive damages and attorney's fees. Under Sec. 10 the act takes effect after mayoral approval or veto override, a 30-day congressional review period, and publication in the District of Columbia Register.

notes: Bill text as introduced; the document shows no bill number or introduction date, and the registry status is pending. Sec. 4(b)(2) ends mid-sentence ('to a part of an affirmative action plan'), and a fragment '(C) make algorithmic eligibility determinations...' runs into Sec. 5, so the text may be incomplete or garbled at that point. Sec. 7(a)(2) lists 'genetic information' as a protected trait that Sec. 4(a)(1) does not list. Sec. 3(4)(D) makes any 'service provider' a covered entity, while Sec. 3(7) defines service provider by reference to performing determinations for another entity. Sec. 2(f) names the 'D.C. Human Rights Act' while Secs. 3(5) and 4(b)(1) cite the Human Rights Act of 1977. Sec. 10 states no effective date; effectiveness depends on Mayor approval, congressional review and publication.

Official Code § 1-206.02(c)(1)), and publication in the District of Columbia Register.
